utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, you are to be concluding your cross-examination now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, and thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I have just a very brief question, a couple of brief questions. Yesterday, we mentioned your statement, the statement of May 22nd, 2006. It was a statement made to the Prosecutor's office. We were discussing paragraph 17, and we had noted that there was a difference between the English version and the B/C/S version. If I understood the things right, the English version is binding and is the original version. So now let's move on to paragraph 18. There again, I will be reading from the B/C/S version. "At the entrance to the apartment building where we had met Natasa there was on the ground floor a military command or HQ. It was some kind of an ABiH army command post. It was a known thing that this was a command post. Soldiers could be seen there at times both in uniform and plain clothes." So, Witness, is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's this dormitory that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you're talking about a command post, and you were actually thinking about that same dormitory that we mentioned yesterday. That exactly is what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So now I'd like to solve this issue of uniforms. In both paragraphs, if you're talking about -- if you're talking about the same dormitory, in paragraph 17 people have no uniforms and in paragraph 18 they're wearing uniforms. So could we reconcile this and find out whether people actually were wearing uniforms or were not wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In both paragraph it says that they were both wearing uniforms and not wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But yesterday, in paragraph 17 we noted that in the English version, which is binding, it is written that they were not wearing uniform, no one was wearing uniforms; whereas in paragraph 18 you're saying that there were some people, soldiers, actually, who were in uniforms and some who were in plain clothes. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, finally, my last question. And I'm trying to save time, so maybe we could manage without displaying any photograph or pictures. If need be, however, we'll ask for something to be called up. Remember the photograph where you actually pointed to the garage and the new buildings? It's an aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So can you tell us approximately what the distance was between the entrance of the alleyway under your building and the place that, according to you, the shots would have originated from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One hundred and fifty metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with my cross-examination, and I thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Witness, how far from the passageway where Adnan was shot was the location where the soldiers were sleeping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifty metres, approximately 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did the soldiers use that passageway where Adnan was shot to get in and out of the rest stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you see any ABiH soldiers in the area when Adnan was shot on the 24th of October, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before this -- Adnan's mishap, no, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was the place where Adnan was shot known to be a dangerous place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a sniper shooting, of course, through the passageway.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were there places in Sarajevo which were notorious snipers' nests?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were any of them in your neighbourhood? Near your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think that the questions that my colleague is now discussing were mentioned during the cross-examination. I don't think that they should be asked during re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would have to agree. I don't think the question of the danger, the relative danger of any particular neighbourhood was asked, though at the end I will ask it because I'm interested in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, on the 24th of October, 1994, was there anything blocking the view between the school for the blind and the spot where your friend Adnan was shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask you, then, if there were particular areas that were known to be dangerous and known to be used by snipers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately the whole of my neighbourhood was dangerous. There were lots of these so-called snipers' nests in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And were there any particular features about your neighbourhood or any other neighbourhood that would make them amenable to sniping?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-62 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A very large part of Sarajevo was under sniper fire. I know about that because I went to school every day. About 8 to 9 kilometres I had to walk through various street passages, behind containers, blankets and things. So I had an opportunity to see a lot of those places, Socijalno, Pofalici, and basically neighbourhoods of that sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness 62, that concludes your testimony. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your next witness, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecutor calls Hendrik Nicolai. Could I ask the Chamber's indulgence for a minute or two so that we can swap seats here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you for giving me the floor. Before our next witness is in the courtroom, I would like to mention one thing, one thing for you to know. I accepted this time yet again for Mr. Nicolai to appear today. I do not wish to slow down the proceedings in any way or to have the Court incurring extra costs. If we have witnesses here and we don't question them, there are certain difficulties that arise. This was also the case with Mr. Mandilovic, and we have the same case now with Mr. Nicolai. As for the statement of the witness that is about to appear, on the 16th through the 20th of October, 2006, the first time I received this was the 18th of January this year, no sooner than that. I received the translation of that statement on Monday, the 21st. The difficulty that I faced was insurmountable, the same as was the case with Mr. Mandilovic. I made an enormous effort to reconcile the two in order to find myself not facing the same difficulty as with Mr. Mandilovic. I gave the statement of the accused on that day and not before. I practically had no opportunity to discuss the statement with the accused. I will not make an issue out of this. But, Your Honours, in order for me to be able to cross-examine this witness, as far as the time allowed me is concerned, please allow me sufficient time so that I may be able to cover all the topics covered in these two statements, to define them all in the best possible way and study any parallels between the two statements, any analogies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How long is this witness scheduled for?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the 65 ter summary the witness is down for one hour. I mentioned to Judge Harhoff this morning that I think he will go longer than that. I have got -- I have added some topics that I want to cover with him since the 65 ter summary was submitted. I should also add that I do not think that will -- not that's what's before the Tribunal right now, but I don't think that will lengthen the Prosecution's case in any way. We will make up the time later in the case and we've got -- we know how we'll be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the witness list, the time listed is two hours; not one hour, two hours. And the other thing is, if we had gone on as envisaged -- however, I do want to ask you one thing: I'm not saying anything. Maybe that will be sufficient time for me, but can you please take that into account? I'm facing a great deal of difficulty going through all of this to ensure that the accused might have a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we will take that into consideration. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may begin, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself to the people in the courtroom by telling us your name and what you do for a living.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not hearing any interpretation. Would you please stop. I regret that I have to interrupt you, but we haven't received any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was saying that I regret to have to interrupt you, but we have not received any interpretation. Would you please repeat what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The position is the same. There appears to be a technical difficulty, and it will take, I am told, just a second. That, no doubt, is an underestimation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is the interpreter. Can you hear the -- good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are now hearing the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm Cornelis Hendrik Nicolai. I'm a retired brigadier general from the Royal Dutch Air Force -- excuse me, the Royal Dutch Army, and I'm here as a witness because in 1995 I was UNPROFOR Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you retired, sir, what was your rank in the Royal Dutch Army?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Brigadier General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that was interpreted properly. I heard Major General from the witness and Brigadier General in my earphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Major General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Major General. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Major General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: You mentioned a minute ago that you served with the United Nations Protection Force, usually referred to as UNPROFOR. Whereabouts in the world were you stationed with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR command was stationed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the headquarters where I served was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What date did you arrive in Sarajevo, and what date did you leave?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I arrived on 23 February 1995. On 28 February, I assumed the position of Chief of Staff, and on 2 September 1995, I subsequently transferred -- transferred again, and on 4 September 1995, I returned to the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During the time -- during the time that you were with UNPROFOR what rank did you hold?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Brigadier General.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Who was your boss?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was the English Lieutenant General Rupert Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And what was Lieutenant General Smith's job in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: He was the UNPROFOR military commander for the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And who did General Smith report to in turn? Who was his boss?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was the UNPF commander; that's the command of the entire former Yugoslavia. That was General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Whereabouts was General Janvier stationed? Where was his headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Going back to General Smith, underneath General Smith, who commanded, you've testified, the Bosnia-Herzegovina command, were there other commanders commanding smaller areas of territory?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In addition to the Bosnia-Herzegovina command, there was a command for the area of Croatia and -- and, as far as I can remember, for Macedonia as well. Altogether there were three subcommanders of General Janvier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right. And underneath General Smith, who commanded Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there subcommanders under Lieutenant General Smith?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. There were three main sectors, the North-East Sector, the South-West Sector, and the Sarajevo Sector. In addition, there was a small command for the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During the time that you were in Bosnia, who was the commander of Sector Sarajevo under General Smith?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was the French Major General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Whereabouts in Sarajevo was General Smith's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was in the centre of Sarajevo, in a building that was referred to as the Residence, and that was located next to the US embassy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: You were with UNPROFOR, United Nations Protection Force. Are you also familiar with the acronym UNMO, U-N-M-O; and if you are, could you tell us what U-N-M-O stands for, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: U-N-M-O stands for United Nations Military Observer. Those were observers from the United Nations who operated unarmed and tried to gain an impression of what was happening within their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I want to talk for a few minutes about these two groups of soldiers, UNPROFOR and UNMO. To begin with, you've described the chain of command for UNPROFOR from General Gobillard to General Smith to General Janvier in Zagreb. Did the UNMOs also -- were they a part of UNPROFOR? Were they separate from it? Did they have a chain of command? Can you comment on those issues, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: They were part of the UNPROFOR command structure despite that they reported to their own line of command. So the UNMOs of UNPROFOR also reported directly to the UNMO UNPF chief in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And did the UNMOs have a headquarters in Sarajevo as well or was that at the Residence with General Smith, or was it somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. The chief UNMO of UNPROFOR was also located in the Residence. The UNMOs themselves were dispersed through the entire area, both in Sarajevo and in the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now that we've, I think, got the command structure identified, I want to talk about what the missions are of these United Nations soldiers. What is the mission, or what was the mission of UNPROFOR at the time that you were with it in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, there were multiple aspects of that mission. First of all, it entailed providing military assistance. UNHCR and the NGOs, the non-governmental organisations, in providing humanitarian aid and in restoring utilities centres. I'll continue in a moment. Next, as we described it in English, it was to secure the safe areas, to maintain and secure the safe areas. And finally, creating conditions to be able to evacuate the wounded and to improve the living conditions of the population, to protect the population, and, if necessary, to end hostilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you say that one of the things UNPROFOR did was protect the population, explain to us, please, how UNPROFOR can do that in a war zone with few soldiers. What techniques are available to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, first you have to try to reach agreements with all the parties and to arrange for them not to attack each other, and next it's the duty of UNPROFOR and the UN units to supervise compliance with these agreements. This starts with the duty of observer, so to observe whether they're complying with the agreements; and in the events of violations of the agreements, then intervention is necessary. That may entail a wide range of measures. The simplest is to issue warnings and write letters of protest. The next step up on the scale is to intervene with military means. For example, if there was firing with small-calibre weapons, then you can try to stop that by returning the fire. In the event of -- in the event that heavier weapons are used, then the UN troops had a problem because they did not have heavier artillery. So if the other side used mortars or artillery, then we didn't have an equivalent level of violence to respond and all we could do was to threaten to deploy air force. And that was the highest step on the scale, which was to deploy the air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I want to talk with you a little bit more about the issue you've just been talking about of a proportionate response. You've testified that because UNPROFOR did not itself have heavy weapons it could not reply in kind to violations when one side or the other used heavy weapons. Have I stated your testimony accurately, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. For a very long time that was the biggest problem of the United Nations. Only after June 1995, when the UN troops were reinforced by the Rapid Reaction Force did we have heavier weaponry at our disposal so that we were able to response more proportionately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Going back to the protest letters or violation letters - I forget the exact term you used, I apologise - what purposes does sending a letter serve when you're talking about a violation of rules of war, an exclusion zone, a cease-fire, what have you? What is the point of sending a letter to another -- to a commander?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's of limited use. It's an official confirmation that carries a bit more authority than a message by phone toward the parties that have violated an agreement. The second purpose concerns registration, because that way we can establish an administrative record as to how often we have warned a certain party about a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Do the letters have any notice or warning function?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As notice, yes, but the letters of protest did not ordinarily list sanctions. Very occasionally this did happen. I remember a warning once that the commander concerned might be summoned before the Tribunal, and in an isolated case, there was threat of a weapon from the air, air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you say that in one case the commander in question was warned that he might face prosecution before an international tribunal, do you remember the name of the commander to whom that letter was sent?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That was General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Let's talk for a minute about how a decision was made within UNPROFOR to send a letter of protest. Let us say that a violation has occurred and the decision is being talked about, should we or should we not make a protest. Could you just walk Their Honours through the internal decision-making process within UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. In the event of violation of an agreement, or if an incident conflicted with international regulations, then the most important staff officers, the heads of the different staff divisions, would meet under the leadership of Smith and with me present and the chief of civil affairs, and we would discuss what had occurred, if it was known what the possible instigation was of that incident, and subsequently which measures were considered to be necessary. And after the UNPROFOR commander had reached a decision, the action was submitted to the Chief of Staff for execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff was yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And what were your duties as Chief of Staff? You've said that General Smith would give you this decision, for you to put it into execution. Is that the sort of thing that the Chief of Staff routinely does day in and day out?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This is the way you should see it: In carrying out his duties, a commander has an extensive staff; in this case, slightly over 100 persons. The staff keeps a record of what happens and evaluates the daily course of events and reports about this to the commander and advises the commander about any decisions this might need to be taken. The day-to-day supervision of the staff is the job of the Chief of Staff who ensures that the duties are performed and the reports are submitted in time and that the operations continue and that the -- that there's manpower 24 hours a day for the staff and that the staff can function.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: With regard to these -- going back now to the protest letters, notice letters, violation letters, how did they get to the commander that they were addressed to? How were they delivered? And let us talk, first of all, about letters being sent to the Bosnian Serb commanders.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The letters to the Bosnian Serb commanders were, depending on their level -- I'll start with -- for example, if Sector Sarajevo sent a letter to the commander of the Bosnian Serb army corps in the Sarajevo division, the letter would be presented to the liaison officer of the Bosnian Serb army whom they could usually reach via the airport. If these were letters from UNPROFOR and concerned the headquarters in Pale of General Mladic, then these letters would be sent by fax to an UNMO post in Pale located next to the headquarters of General Mladic, and UNMOs would then present the letter to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: How was it decided whether a letter would be sent to the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps or to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That depended on how serious the incident was. Minor violations of the agreements, in those cases General Gobillard would protest directly to the army corps. And if there were serious incidents, this could happen at the request of General Gobillard, or based on the assessment of General Smith, the report would go to a higher level, that of the Bosnian Serb army, so to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you yourself write protest letters during your time in Sarajevo, or sign protest letters might be the better way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, many. I estimate that I wrote over 50 protest letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I want to look at some examples of those protest letters now, General, and I'll ask the registrar to please --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour. If the registrar could please display on the monitor 65 ter number 2851.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Who is this letter addressed to, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This letter is addressed to Lieutenant General Milovanovic, and he was the deputy of General Mladic. Ordinarily, he was my most common point of contact at the headquarters in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And was that a protocol, that a chief of staff would correspond with a chief of staff, a division commander with a division commander?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This was very strictly observed to avoid skipping levels and everything going directly to the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if I could ask the registrar to scroll down to the signature block on this letter, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: From that signature block, can you tell who signed this letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I don't see a signature there, but I do see my name, and I recognise the letter. So this is, indeed, a letter of protest that I sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What's the date of the letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: 17 April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if we could scroll back up so that the text of the letter is displayed, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: The letter speaks for itself. I'm not going to ask you to read it out loud, but what is the context of this letter? What is this letter reacting to? What is the situation that has caused this letter to be sent?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: From time to time shots might be fired at incoming aeroplanes at Sarajevo airport. Of course, responses were sent immediately to try to end this. In certain cases, especially the arrival of important visitors, it was emphasised additionally to the fighting parties that an important person would be arriving, and we demanded guarantees as to the safety of the incoming aircraft.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you receive a response to this letter; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I don't remember anymore, but I assume that I received an affirmative response because the visit proceeded without problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document, 65 ter number 2851 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit P101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, I now want to talk about another protest letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And I would ask the registrar to please display on the screen a document bearing 65 ter number 2322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just ask the Brigadier something? Just going back to the last letter that you sent, the letter of protest, did you understand the LO's reply that he could not guarantee the safety of the aircraft to mean that there was a possibility that Serb forces might fire at that aircraft?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Getting back to the answer I provided earlier, I don't remember exactly the response that we received. I do remember that the visit from the US ambassador proceeded, and I infer from that that there were guarantees issued as to the safety of the aircraft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But what I was asking is, if you were told that their safety could not be guaranteed, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at least that the ambassador concerned would be consulted as to whether the risk should be taken to land in Sarajevo without those guarantees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Just following up on His Honour's question, was there some indication before this letter was sent that Serbian forces might shoot down an aircraft containing an ambassador, or fire upon it at least?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I no longer know exactly what the reason was, but after some fairly quiet months at the beginning of 1995, as of early April, the violations of the agreement in place at the time regarding cessation of hostilities, the violations started to increase. So the number of firing incidents increased as well as firing incidents in the area of the airport. And I assume that one of those incidents was the reason why we requested a guarantee for the safety of the aircraft concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: You mentioned in that answer, General, that the first few months of 1995 had been - I believe I'm quoting your words, at least in the English translation - "fairly quiet." Can you give us something more specific? When you say "fairly quiet" in the context of Sarajevo in 1995, let me ask it this way: Did the UNMOs, the United Nations Military Observers, log firing incidents on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. When I say "fairly quiet," and under peace conditions you might find this a bit strange, I mean anything from no firing incidents to a few hundred firing incidents. And that may come across as rather remarkable, but as a basis for comparison, I can tell you that in May and June more than a few thousand firing incidents happened in a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now let's turn to the letter that's on the screen. Can you tell us to whom this letter is addressed?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Also to Lieutenant General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If I could ask the registrar to please scroll down to the signature block.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, can you tell us who has signed that letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: My signature appears at the bottom of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could I ask the registrar to please scroll up so we can see as much of the text as will fit into the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with this letter? Do you remember this letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: It looks familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And if you need to take a moment to read it over, that's fine. Then I'll have a few questions about it. Just say yes when you're ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I am. Yes, I have read the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: You indicate here in the first sentence that "Over the last two months, an increasing number of heavy weapon violations," et cetera, et cetera. What form did these heavy weapon violations take?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In general, these were shellings with mortars or with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What restrictions had been placed upon heavy weapons? Can you just tell us in a couple, three, sentences what the restrictions were on heavy weapons and how firing a mortar violates those restrictions? I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In the safe areas we had the so-called exclusion zones. Within these exclusion zones, the warring factions were not allowed to have heavy weapons at their disposal. All heavy weapons that were present in these exclusion zones would be gathered in the so-called weapon collection points and were held there under surveillance of UN Military Observers. The warring factions, however, did have access to these heavy weapons, and they did have permission to conduct maintenance whenever necessary. However, this would always take place under the supervision of UN personnel. Nevertheless, from time to time there were cases of abuse of this permission, and the heavy weapons would be used, would be fired in the direction of the adversary. In other cases there were attempts to remove weaponry from the weapon collection points and to transfer them to their own held territory outside the exclusion zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And if I could ask the registrar now to just scroll up for a moment to the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, could you tell us the date of this letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The 26th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Following this letter being sent, did this end the problems with the heavy weapon exclusion zones or did they continue?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately, after this, several similar events took place several times, and as a result, at the end of May the UN formulated an ultimatum to the Bosnian Serb army to withdraw heavy weapons under the threat of the use of the air force, and this threat materialised in the end on 25th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Following the -- well, first of all, on the 25th of May, if you remember, what was hit by the air-strike?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The target of the air-strikes was an ammunition complex in the vicinity of Pale, and specifically chosen in the vicinity of Pale because that was where the headquarters of the Bosnian Serb army was located. We chose an ammunition storage because this was a purely military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Was there a response from the Bosnian Serb authorities or the Bosnian Serb army to this air-strike on the ammunition depot in Pale? And if the answer is yes, would you describe that reaction to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic issued a furious reaction to this air-strike. He considered it to be completely unjust, and he accused United Nations of having touched a school and a hospital as well in this air attack, which was absolutely not the case given the fact that the ammunition storage was located outside inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Beyond General Mladic's angry words, was there any further response?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there was. In reaction to the use of air force, there was a number of retaliation measures that, however not announced as such, were experienced by the UN as such. There were cases of shooting on the enclaves of Bihac, Gorazde. There was a terrible case of shelling of the centre of the city of Tuzla with over 80 civilian casualties, not aiming at any military object but firing at the centre of town. There were similar indents of shooting in a number of other cities where non-military targets were fired upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Was there anything directed at the United Nations as such?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I'm not completely sure. I believe that the Tuzla airport has been touched as well, but I cannot recall that with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What would that have to do with the United Nations in relation to the specific question? You were asked whether there was anything directed at the United Nations, and your answer was that you're not completely sure, but you believed that the Tuzla airport was touched. Is there a connection between the Tuzla airport and the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My apologies. I should have explained this. On the Tuzla airport, the Sector North-East headquarters of the UN was situated. There were UN troops at the airport in order to guard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, I'm now going to move on. Before I do leave this protest letter, were protest letters, on occasion, sent to the Bosnian Muslim armed forces commanders as well?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This happened as well, although this was quite a bit easier given the fact that there were headquarters of the BiH army in Sarajevo itself. Therefore, it was much easier to convey them. At the same time, with some frequency, a liaison officer of the same army would visit the UN headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Another question more or less of clarification. We've been looking at the English text of these letters. Were they sent in languages other than English?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They would be sent both in Serbian and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have on this letter, Your Honour. I would ask that this document 65 ter number 2322 be entered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P102, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And may I please ask the registrar to put on the screen the next letter. It bears 65 ter number 2498.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Do you see the letter in front of you, General, on the screen?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and by now I have read it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: All right. First of all, who has signed this letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This letter bears my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What is the date of this letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The letter bears the date of 1st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And thirdly, to whom is this letter addressed?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This letter is addressed to General Mladic, and this is a letter in support of letters of protest previously sent by the Sector Sarajevo given the graveness of the violations of the agreements, in this case by shootings into the city of Sarajevo where civilian casualties took place. Therefore, this letter was sent to the headquarters in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And we will get -- I'm sorry. We will get to the contents of the letter in just a moment, General, but before we do that, I understood from your testimony so far that you typically corresponded with your opposite number, Chief of Staff Lieutenant General Manojlo Milovanovic, and yet here we see a letter to General Ratko Mladic over your signature. Could you explain how it came to be that in this case the protocol was not followed and that you wrote to General Mladic rather than General Smith writing to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I don't know why this letter was not signed by General Smith. It might be that at that time he was not present at the headquarters. However, given the seriousness of the violations in this case, the letter was specifically addressed to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Just to follow up on your last answer, if General Smith was not in Sarajevo, would you have the authority to write a letter like this on your own initiative?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I would have this authority. However, in fact, looking at that date, I see indeed that General Smith at that date was not present. Whenever General Smith would not be present, he would be replaced by General Gobillard; therefore, General Gobillard might have signed this letter. However, I assume that we wanted to underscore that this letter was coming from another level in the military structure and that therefore it was decided I would sign the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now, this letter, in its text, in the third paragraph, refers to a copy of a letter of protest from acting commander Sector Sarajevo. We're going to look at the copy of the letter from the acting commander in a moment, but from that title, "Acting Commander," can you tell or make any conclusions about whether General Gobillard was in Sarajevo when the letter was written?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: If Colonel Meille, who was Chief of Staff of the Sector Sarajevo, would have sign the letter as acting commander, this would imply that at that time General Gobillard was not present at the headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I ask the registrar, there should be a second page to this 65 ter number. Could we see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Do you see that in front of you, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we see the signature block, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Who has signed the letter, General?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Colonel Meille, in this case in the capacity as acting sector commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we see the date on the letter at the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What date did General Meille send this letter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: On the 30th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: To whom is the letter addressed?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This letter is addressed to Major General Milosevic, the corps commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: In the last paragraph that appears on that page -- well, it's no longer the last paragraph on that page. Do you see the paragraph that begins: "The seriousness of the events of the past 48 hours ..."?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And do you see the last line of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Is that last line the reference to a trial by an international court that you testified about at the beginning of your testimony when you were summarising the sorts of protest letters that were sent?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This is a very clear example of such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is a leading question, to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't agree at all, because the witness had earlier testified about a statement that he made in relation to the possibility of trial by an international court, and the counsel here is seeking to have that confirmed. But I wanted to find out from the witness whether his protest letter to General Mladic was prompted by the same attacks on the 28th and 29th that were the subject of the letter that we are now looking at to General Milosevic, or was it concerned with other violations?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, other witnesses have testified about the text of this letter, and I was not going to lead the witness through the text. Rather, I think this witness, what he adds is the discussions between himself and Colonel Meille over how the decision was made to send these letters, and I believe that -- I believe, without giving testimony myself, that that will be responsive to Your Honour's questions as to why this witness sent the letter that we saw a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he must be in a position to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, he is -- I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe he should be in a position to say. What I want to find out, simply, is whether the violations that were the subject matter of his protest letter to General Mladic were confined to the same violations that were the subject matter of General Meille's letter, or whether they were wider.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The letter concerned the very same violations as to ones on which Mr. Meille had written. Given the seriousness of the violations, Colonel Meille asked me to send a letter of protest to General Mladic as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, what I wanted to ask you to describe to the Court -- this letter is in evidence through earlier witnesses. However, what I would like you to talk to the Court about, and what they have not heard about yet, were there discussions between you and Colonel Meille before these two letters that we've looked at were sent respectively to General Mladic and General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I don't remember any discussions about that. Basically it's an extremely reasonable request from Sector Sarajevo in the event of such serious violations, to ask the UNPROFOR headquarters to send a letter of protest as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And I apologise. Perhaps my question was not clear. But I think you answered the question I should have asked, which is did you send this at the request of Sarajevo? Your letter, I mean.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, these letters were sent in the normal way for delivery, either by fax to Pale or -- in the case of General Mladic, or by delivery to the liaison officer, in the case of General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, because there were no other channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When you sent protest letters - and now I'm speaking generally, not about the protest letter on the screen - when you sent these protest letters, did you get responses?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Usually I did. Not always in writing. Sometimes the responses arrived by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Was there any response that was made so often or so frequently that you could characterise it as a typical response?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the responses consisted of denials. It was generally denied that the actions stated had been performed by the parties concerned. Other times it was said that the actions had been performed but that they were a response to provocation by the other side. Those were the most common answers provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then the last protest letter I would like to look at, I'd ask the registrar to please call up 65 ter number ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- the witness. You say that some of the responses indicated that the action was a response to provocation by the other side. I'm interested in that. Can you say whether those responses to provocation, whether there was a factual basis for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was indeed the case sometimes. Each time violations occurred, we tried to find out from the UNMOs which party had started the violation, and in some cases it was indeed true that not the Bosnian Serb army had started but the Bosnian Muslims had started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that in some cases it was a matter of fact that the violations which you allege the Serb army committed were responsive to action taken by the Bosnian Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. These could be both violations with small-calibre arms as well reactions to firing heavier weaponry. And obviously we contacted the parties that had committed these acts about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether, in this responsive action by the Bosnian Serb army, any casualties were sustained, in particular whether any civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the case concerned in this letter, there were indeed civilian casualties as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And may I ask, Mr. Docherty, whether the particular incidents referred to in this letter are the subject of any allegation in the indictment; and, if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll have to double-check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'll need to check, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: But I'm capable of giving a more general response, which is that the scheduled incidents, of course, are illustrative examples. Even if these were not scheduled in the indictment, the Prosecution's view is that we lead evidence on incidents over -- many more incidents over and above those scheduled. The ones that are scheduled, our view is that we prove those beyond a reasonable doubt as illustrative examples. But I will certainly check on the break and be able to give you a response. Excuse me just a moment. Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I do see a number of paragraphs referred to in relation to this witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. And, yes, the incidents referred to on the 28th of June are indeed in the schedule to the indictment. They are scheduled incidents -- shelling incidents 15 and 16. And then there is also in the indictment a rocket bomb that was fired on the 29th of June, 1995, incident number 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, I would like to ask you about a question of your responses to the warring parties. Now, we have mostly this morning dealt with how and when reactions from the United Nations were offered to the Serbian side. You have also testified that frequently the shooting was initiated by the Bosnian side. My question would, therefore, be: Would you also then present letters of protest to the Bosnian army when you became aware of violations occurring from the Bosnian side? And how were those protests made, if any? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Letters of protest were indeed written to the BiH, which was the Bosnian Muslim army, although this was the case less frequently than toward the Bosnian Serb army. The texts corresponded with the text in the letters you already saw. And in one case I remember that in mid-May the violations occurred so frequently at that we actually convened a meeting with Minister Silajdzic and with the leaders of the Bosnian Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm now going to move from the topic of protest letters to the topic of sniping, shelling, and air bombs. Before I do that, may I put something on the record concerning this witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this witness began testifying, counsel for the Defence indicated that he had only recently received statements of this witness. We have been checking that, and I don't know what happened. We will have to check with the Defence. Our disclosure records indicate that the English version of the statement in question was disclosed on 1 November 2006, and the B/C/S version of that statement on 22 November 2006. I would also note for the record that the disclosure of exhibits which the Defence intends to use with General Nicolai was received by us in the course of his direct examination at eight minutes past 10.00. Perhaps at the break counsel and I could confer and see why their dates are different from ours. But our dates indicate that this was turned over two and a half months before counsel indicates he received it. So there's something there that we will need to check into.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. There's an element of confusion somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you would allow me, before you move on to another topic, I would like to ask the witness. With regard to the missions of the UNPROFOR, are you aware of the criticism levelled at the UNPROFOR? It was said that the UNPROFOR simply took care of distributing humanitarian aid, whereas the population was facing the most horrible suffering. But if I've understood you correctly and understood your explanations correctly, you mentioned among the missions of the UNPROFOR the creation of conditions that would be conducive to an end to hostilities. And that point, the end of hostilities, is of interest to me. What do you mean exactly by creating conditions conducive to ending hostilities? Do you mean military conditions, military pressure brought to bear on the warring parties, or do you mean discussions and negotiations that, to my mind, were being carried out by politicians? And more concretely, what exactly did the UNPROFOR do in relation, for example, to the presumed or alleged shots fired by snipers knowing that those shots were known by the -- or often coming from the headquarters in Sarajevo, that is alleged to be the Serbian forces? So what would be the position of the UNPROFOR vis-a-vis those sniping incidents? Of course, letters to exert pressure would be useful, but were other measures undertaken upstream?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't provide you with a brief answer to this question, but I'll try to provide you with the most accurate possible response. Of course, when violations occurred, we also tried to negotiate to end those hostilities. These negotiations were conducted both by military people from UNPROFOR and by the civil division, which was known as civil affairs. If this didn't help and if letters of protest didn't help, then UNPROFOR also had military means at its disposal to retaliate against hostilities. Very specifically, when sniping incidents occurred and when snipers fired, then we would fire back using UNPROFOR military means. We had certain hot spots, dangerous sites. At these dangerous sites we had set up armoured vehicles that had heavy machine-guns or lighter arms to fire back at the places where parties had fired from. There were also patrols in certain areas, and as needed we returned fire toward places that firing came from. It was more difficult to respond to the use of heavy arms, first of all, because the firing distance was larger in those cases; second, because UNPROFOR did not have means that matched the level of violence. UNPROFOR did not have heavy mortars or artillery. The only response were means -- that we could use to retaliate in those cases was through air-strikes. Only then there's a problem as to proportionality. If one mortar is fired from a backyard, then it's difficult, first of all, to find that target; and second, considering the impact of air-strikes, the danger of collateral damage, as it's known, so damage to the surroundings of a target, is immense. To put it very simply, you can't burn down a residential area just to neutralise one mortar. And that was generally the problem that UNPROFOR faced during those months. Only after the repatriation forces occurred and were able to localise the area -- the Rapid Reaction Forces, excuse me, they were able to use very accurate artillery to provide a more adequate response, but that was after July and August of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are at the break time. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, I understand you have some matters you wish to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Two very brief matters, Your Honour. The. First is by way of a heads-up to the Chamber. As the Chamber knows, the Prosecution has applied for protective measures for a number of its witnesses. I am not going to mention this witness by name, of course, to avoid the need for going into private or closed session, but it has been brought to my attention by a colleague who is perhaps more assiduous than I that one of these witnesses, number 138, was previously granted the protections we are seeking in an earlier proceeding before this Tribunal. I will put this in writing later today, but the oral order in question was issued and 6 December 2001 and is found at page 862 of the transcript of the Prosecutor versus Galic. As I say, I just wanted to put that on the record immediately, but I will follow up in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And I would take this opportunity to raise some other administrative matters in relation to motions for admission of written statements pursuant to Rules 92 bis and ter filed by the Prosecution on the 11th of January. The Defence response is, therefore, due by the 25th of January, which is tomorrow. One of the witnesses mentioned in the motion is scheduled to testify on Thursday, the 25th. That's tomorrow. And three more are scheduled to testify on Monday the 29th. And these are the witnesses concerned: Sanela Dedovic, scheduled for Thursday, 25th January. Therefore, we would want the response of the Defence by this afternoon. Huso Palo, scheduled for Monday, the 29th; we would want that response by tomorrow. Sabina Sabanic, scheduled for Monday, the 29th; we would want the Defence response by tomorrow. Kemal Buco, scheduled for Monday, the 29th; we would want the Defence response by tomorrow. Proceed, Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: As the first matter of business, Your Honour, I offer into evidence 65 ter number 2498. That is the package of protest letters from the witness and Colonel Meille to General Milosevic and General Mladic that we were looking at just before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be admitted as Exhibit P103, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Major General, before the break we were discussing incidents of heavy weapons, exclusion zone violations, and a NATO air-strike on an ammunition depot in Pale that resulted. Do you remember the questions and answers that you and I had along those lines?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember what I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And, General, I then asked you about responses directed against the United Nations itself, and your answer concerned the airport at Tuzla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next question will be leading, but I do it because I am obliged by the rules to put my case to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Major General, was there also an incident of hostage-taking?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: If you're talking about those dates, 28 and 29 June, I don't remember any case of hostage-taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object, Your Honours, to the question thus formulated, and I'm expecting you to decide on this issue. It's been demonstrated from the answer that it is correct, but I don't think that these kinds of questions are permissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me hear Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If it simplifies the Chamber's decision, I don't intend to go any further. I have done what the Rules require me to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Remind me of the Rule. Is it Rule 90 or 80?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: It's Rule 98, Your Honour -- I'm sorry, 90(H) as in "Hotel," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what is the particular section?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour, while I get a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: 90(H) deals with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I could also withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Rule 90(H) does not provide a basis for a leading question. What it does, it allows a party in cross-examination to question a witness in relation to evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party. So I uphold the submission made by Mr. Tapuskovic that the question was leading. But I note that you have withdrawn it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Or you may get to it by some other means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I know I tendered those letters, Your Honour. Were they received? Ter number 2498?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: They were admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Major General, I'm now going to move away from the subject of protest letters and UNPROFOR structure and go into questions of shelling and sniping and air bombs. To begin with, how many years did you spend in the Dutch armed forces before you retired?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Thirty-nine years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During your 39 years with the Dutch army, did you have experience with mortars?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. For nearly two years I was deputy commander of a mortar company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During your time -- based on your experience, your professional experience, with mortars, does the phrase "register a target" have a professional meaning to you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It means that you can shoot at targets with a mortar so that you can fire very accurately at your target.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Chamber how a mortar is registered upon a particular target.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: As it happens, it follows before you shoot at the target with an entire firing unit or platoon, you start by firing with a single piece of artillery. You fire one shot which is observed by an observer, and that observer then indicates where the grenade has landed with respect to the target and then indicates the correction necessary to get the shot -- to make the shot more accurate or to get it closer to the target. That is repeated as many times as necessary until the grenade reaches the exact target. And after that, all other items of the firing unit are directed in the same manner, and that guarantees that the fire of all those firing units reach the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Once a mortar has been registered upon a target, does the mortar crew need to see the target in order to hit it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: So they could hit the target at night or through fog, for example?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. If no corrections have been made, then that's possible. The only corrections that might be necessary would be the consequence of changes in the wind speed, but you can do that by measuring the wind speed and by consulting tables. You needn't see the target for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Did you have an understanding, based upon your time with UNPROFOR in Sarajevo, about the length of time that some of the Serbian army mortars had been in a single position in the hills overlooking Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I apologise, but I didn't completely understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: It was a very long question. Let me try and break it down. If a mortar -- hypothetically, if a mortar is in one location for a long period of time, can it be accurately registered on a target?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes is the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And did you have an understanding as to how long some of the Serbian army mortars had been in an unmoved position in the hills overlooking Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I do not know when those positions were taken, but throughout the period that I served in Sarajevo those positions were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now, when you say that those positions were occupied, can you tell the Chamber what opportunity you had to observe those positions, to see those positions?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I was able to observe some of those positions even from the headquarters. This was possible because Sarajevo is in a valley surrounded by hills, and most of the positions of the Bosnian Serbs were on those hills. Perhaps I was unable to observe other positions personally, but they were observable from the positions at the UNMOs, the UN observers. Then I was able to see a number of positions. I visited the headquarters in Pale once, and the road to Pale took me past a few of those positions, so I saw them from very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: During your time with the Dutch army as deputy commander of a mortar company, did you learn how to distinguish a good mortar crew from a mortar crew that maybe wasn't so good?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion about the quality of the Serbian army mortar crews that were in the hills overlooking Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: It was my impression, I say this with some reserve, my impression was that they were very professional. My reserve -- my reservation concerned the aspect I was unable to assess. The quality of a mortar crew or company is determined, in part, by the speed at which they are able to take position and to fire at a certain target. Because the positions had been occupied for some time and that registration had taken place much earlier, I was therefore not able to assess that aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: What aspect were you able to observe? If you weren't able to observe the speed with which they set up and opened fire, what could you look at?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The accuracy with which targets were shot at, which was generally very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And were some of these targets, some of these things that were hit by mortars, civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Sometimes civilian targets were indeed shot at. It's difficult to determine whether that was deliberate in all cases or whether it was a missed shot. But considering the quality of the Bosnian Serb forces, when that happened, it was deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to a different type of weapon. Do you know what I mean by the phrase "modified air bomb"?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I understand that you would like me to explain that. In addition to normal conventional artillery and mortars, the Bosnian Serb army also had an improvised device that could be launched to shoot an air bomb driven by a rocket attached to that bomb. Because this was an improvised firing system, this appears to have been a highly inaccurate weapon, but nonetheless a weapon with extremely high explosive force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And during your time with the Dutch army, did you learn the different types of weapons that are suited to different types of battlefield situations?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Does the modified air bomb that you have just described have -- would a commander ever turn to a modified air bomb in a battlefield situation?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Only in a situation where they wanted to cause very heavy damage and in a situation where accuracy is of secondary importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Do you have an opinion as to why or what use these modified air bombs were put by the Bosnian Serb army in Sarajevo? What was the purpose of firing them?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The only thing I can imagine is that, considering the impact of the projectile, it had a type of deterrent effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: How did it deter?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Because it causes heavy material damage, and there is also a chance that there will be high casualties resulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Earlier, before the break, the Chamber asked you about whether any of the fire directed on Sarajevo by the Bosnian Serb army was a response to provocation and you answered yes. Do you remember that exchange with the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I remember those answers. I stated very specifically that in some cases there was provocation, but not in all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: When there was provocation, could you describe to the Bench what a typical provocation would be?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: A provocation might be shooting with small-calibre weapons at the Serb positions. Another type of provocation might be shooting with heavy arms. It's known, among other things, that open-roofed vehicles were used to which a mortar was attached; that it would fire from arbitrary -- well, not arbitrary, but at various sites outside the city at Bosnian Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Was the response by the Bosnian Serb army proportionate to these provocations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. He must say what the response was, not to say whether it was proportionate. We will determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: General, let us take some examples in response to mortar rounds being fired by the Bosnian Muslims, what sort of response or, if there was a range, what range of responses did you observe from the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Usually such rounds would be followed by shooting on different targets in town. I would consider something proportional that would aim the position from which the one side has initiated firing. However, very often this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said earlier that I would not allow you to say whether it was proportionate. Just tell us what the response was as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. The reaction, as I mentioned, usually would be that there would be return fire on different targets in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Would this include civilian targets in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And then lastly, sniper fire. During your time in Sarajevo, were inhabitants of the city of Sarajevo hit by small-arms fire?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. This would happen with a very high frequency.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And I said "inhabitants." Perhaps I should specify. Were these civilian inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This would concern both civilian inhabitants and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Were there areas of the city of Sarajevo that were well known or notorious as places where civilians could get shot?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, there were such areas. These were the places where the confrontation lines were at a short distance. For instance, the part of the city of Sarajevo where the confrontation line was very close to the centre of town was a place where it was very easy to shoot at the other side at a short range. Another example was the area of the Sarajevo airport where a Serbian neighbourhood was situated at a very short distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And then the last question I have goes back to the protest letters that were sent. We saw that protest letters were sent to General Mladic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: My apologies. Could you repeat the question once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Certainly. We saw earlier some of the protest letters that were sent, and we saw that some of those letters were sent to General Ratko Mladic. Do you recall seeing those letters earlier today on the monitor?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: Now, letters sent to General Mladic, General Mladic is the superior officer of the accused, Dragomir Milosevic; is that correct? Or was at that time.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
