utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHTERY
utterances.text: And by sending letters to General Mladic, was that in any way indicating that you were not holding General Milosevic also accountable for the actions of the troops under his command?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. A commander is always accountable for the acts of the soldiers under his command; however, at the same time his superiors are accountable as well. And in case of serious incidents, we held the opinion that we should also address the superiors of General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. General, may I just ask you one last question in relation to the protest letters that you sent to various commanders on both sides, and my question is if the responses that you received were issued by the same persons to whom you had addressed the protest letters. In other words, did those to whom the protests were addressed reply back to you directly, or did the replies come from somebody else; and, if so, then who responded to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very difficult to confirm this for all cases. In general, the answer would come from the person the letter had been addressed to. However, it would also occur that the person in question would not be present at headquarters. In those cases, on behalf of this person, his acting officer would reply. And this has happened as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. The first thing I would like to say is I intend to examine this witness based of these principal documents. I'm talking about DD00-0287, which is the statement provided by the witness on the 16th, the 23rd, the 25th of October, and the 18th of November, 1996, which means a mere year after the Dayton Accords. That will be the first document. The other document that I will have to be drawing analogies with all the time is DD00-03-19. This document is related to the statement that the witness gave between the 16th and 20th of October, 2006. I will not be addressing any of the problems that I indicated a while ago. Believe me, though, I wish that I was wrong. I wish that I had -- I wish that it had not been the case that I received the translation of this document two days ago, which was the same day that the accused Dragomir Milosevic received it on. But I will not be opening -- I will not be opening that question now. I would like to move on straight to my cross-examination. Once the witness has looked at the documents, I will be pointing him to the exact page numbers in the English with great accuracy. Can we please have this document DD00-0319, dated the 16th through the 20th of October, 2006. I would like to go to page 1 of that document. I'm not sure if the witness has that in front of him already or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this document in evidence, or is it being used for the first time? Mr. Docherty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document would have been moved into evidence had the witness testified 92 ter, but since he did not, no, we did not put the statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Yes, go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, I am Branislav Tapuskovic, attorney-at-law from Belgrade. I would like to ask you a number of questions in relation to your statements. I will be showing you perhaps two or three documents, and one thing I would like to tell you is this: Time is of the essence. Whenever possible, wherever possible, please provide brief answers, yes or no answers, if at all possible. I would like to start with page 1, some general questions. I believe you should be able to provide brief answers. Paragraph 1, you say: "I have previously provided a statement ... which I have read and agree with." This is the statement you provided back in 1996. I will be asking questions about that one, too. Do you still abide by the position expressed here?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 2, at page 1, you also say that you spent your military career in the infantry and that you have some experience with mortar units. I would like to ask you, does that mean that you are exceptionally familiar with mortars, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. I stated before that I have been the deputy commander of a mortar company.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You go on to say that you were General Smith's Chief of Staff. In paragraph 3 you say that meetings occurred in a certain way, and then you say: "... even for discussions with ministers, he was always with me," a colleague of yours. "Although I was Chief of Staff to General Smith, he sometimes had private meetings without my presence." Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you remember, and that's my question, did meetings like that take place at the same time as the dreadful incident occurred at Markale on the 28th of August, 1995? On occasions like that, would he meet anyone privately?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I don't know which incidents you're referring to, but it would happen regularly that General Smith himself, not accompanied by me, would engage in negotiations with ministers of the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Witness, sir, the Prosecutor asked you nothing about what happened on the 28th of August when a shell explode at Markale, or that's what the indictment claims, causing a great number of casualties. I was asking you about that time, the 28th, the 29th, especially the 28th. Were there any meetings held by General Smith, private meetings, face-to-face meetings?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Not as far as I can recall. I have been present at all discussions that took place internally with staff chaired by General Smith on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go back to that once we get to Markale. I have a number of questions about that. In paragraph 4 of your statement, you talk about Mohatarem, a Pakistani lieutenant colonel. You commended his credibility. You say that he was an honourable man. You believe that Mohatarem was an honourable officer at the time. That is at least what your description, provided in your statement, implies.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any facts that would undermine the credibility of the officer in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I thank you. That was my impression, too, during his appearance. I just wanted to see whether you shared my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to move on to the other statement that the witness provided in 1996, on the 25th, if that can be brought up on the screen. DD00-0287, this is the 1996 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you a number of questions about that once you have that on the screen in front you, sir. Page 1, I'm talking about page 1. Sir, do you have that in front of you, page 1 of that statement?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of that statement -- based on paragraph 2 of that statement, can we say that your first international task as a professional soldier in the service of the UN was the one you discharged with UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not even a question. It's precisely what the document reads. "My first international post ..." that's the first sentence of paragraph 2. "My first international post was with the United Nations in UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia." Is what it says true?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The document goes on to state that you volunteered for that mission, for going to that sort of front. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Unless you really have something to add.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, I have nothing -- I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Up until that point in time, you came to this country which at the time was quite a large country. How familiar were you with the country? How much did you really know about the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Of course I took a professional interest in what happened in the Balkans, and from the start of the conflict I followed the reports. I read books about it. And prior to my deployment, I was, of course, briefed about the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this course that you took was a month-long course - that's what your statement suggests - from the moment you had been informed that you would be sent to Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. It was a two-week course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain this, sir, or rather, explain to the Chamber: Since you volunteered for this mission, can you please explain your reason for going to a dangerous place like that of your own freewill? What was the reason behind that decision, your decision to go to an area like that? Was it because of what you had read about the sufferings of the people of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: My reason was twofold. First, shortly before, I had been offered a position that I did not wish to accept for personal reasons, and I requested a different position at that point. I answered that I would be happy to be deployed, first of all, because I had not had that experience and thought the experience would be extremely useful; and second, for ideological reasons, I wanted to contribute to ending the atrocities taking place at that time in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These atrocities occurring in the Balkans, based on what you knew at the time, the Serbs were the sole perpetrators, right, at the time? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. It is definitely not my opinion that only one party was to blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, but what about your experience after you had returned? Is that what the conclusion is based on? What was your conviction when you first set out to go to the area, that all the parties were responsible? Or did you believe at the time that the Serbs were the open ones perpetrating these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Both prior to my deployment and after my deployment, I believed, and continued to believe, that multiple parties were to blame for the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In that case, I will be dropping some of the questions that I was about to ask you. I would like to ask you this next, sir: How much did you really know before your arrival about the victims and casualties on the other side in terms of specific information? Did you have any idea about that, sir, or is the answer the same as before, in which case you needn't even answer.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: This is a very difficult question to answer. What I knew about the conflict was what I had read about it and also what I'd seen during a previous position prior to my deployment to Bosnia, during my visits, what I'd seen there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just as a matter of information, Mr. Docherty, is it the Prosecution's case that the Serbs were the only perpetrators of violence?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, of course not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: This accused was a Serbian general, and that, of course, is where our evidence takes us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Defence might want to take note of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I will not be insisting on this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, what about all those things that you had learned a thing or two before your arrival? Had you, above all, not been told by your predecessor about these things, General Van Baal? Is it not true, sir, that you had heard a great deal about these things from him, of all people? Let me refresh your memory. Let's not dwell on this. I have to go back to the previous document. Unfortunately, I have to take that course of action. DD00-10319, paragraph 24 of that document, please. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, not yet. I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you? I will have to go through it slowly. "I recall that it was very important that the source of fire be determined, because we did not rule out any possibility, including the possibility that the Bosniaks had shelled their own people. I have never seen or have any evidence that the Bosniaks shelled their own people, although I had heard from my predecessor, General Van Baal, that it might have happened during his time there. Elements to consider were ..." And then what follows is not related to this incident. However, I'm talking about what you heard from Van Baal, the way you describe it here. There were cases, apparently, at least that's what the statement says -- or rather, he says the Bosniaks shelled their own people. Is this something that he ever told you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just wrap this up. The Bosnians were shelling their own people and then the whole world saw that as a result of the bombs that the Serbs had been using. Would this be a fair way of putting it, or do you look at this differently, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No. This is, at any rate, what was presumed to have been the intention, shooting at their own troops to give the impression that it was the other party's fault. Excuse me, at people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I look at your statement and see that you arrived in Sarajevo on the 23rd of February, 1995. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need to have the witness clarify what he meant when he said, "This is, at any rate, what was presumed to have been the intention, shooting at their own troops to give the impression that it was the other party's fault." Could you elaborate on that for me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will. General Van Baal, who was actually my predecessor's predecessor, told me before my departure that in one specific case they had a very strong impression that the Bosnian Muslim forces had fired at their own people with the intention of shifting the blame towards the Bosnian Serbs. And I'm formulating it because it was very strongly his impression that that was the way it happened. They never had 100 per cent evidence of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This was information, you say, from your predecessor's predecessor. When was he in Bosnia? What period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was during the first half of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the interpretation into B/C/S that I caught was about shelling their own soldiers, and the statement reads, the portion that I read back to the General, that the Bosniaks were shelling their own people, which means their own civilians, not soldiers. That is the gist of what I've been going on about. It's quite specific, the quote from the statement, "shelled their own people" or "shelling their own people."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we clarify that? Did they shell the front line where the soldiers were or the city itself?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: It concerned the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you arrived when you arrived, and you left on the 2nd of September, 1995. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you left for Bosnia, given your position at the time, you had been told that you would be going there and that you would be arriving just as a cease-fire was taking effect that had begun in January and was supposed to go on until April. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we then say that it's also true that it was from the NATO intelligence sources and NATO security sources that you had found out about the fact that, although there was a cease-fire, the Muslims had already started to prepare for launching an offensive at some later date? Is this something you were familiar with or something that you were told at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I was not informed that there were preparations underway for an offensive. I was informed that the agreement was being violated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you at least tell me whether you knew that throughout there had been negotiations with the representatives of the BH army and the representatives of the army of the Republika Srpska for that agreement to be extended? The Serbs were in favour of an indefinite extension, a lasting or permanent extension, and the Muslims -- I'm sorry. I'm sorry, I apologise, it's really difficult to say Muslims, Bosniaks, Bosnians. Errors like that probably must be made by the situation here, but I will simply have to say, no dilemma at all. I don't think it's a bad thing to describe someone as a Muslim or a Serb or whatever. Nevertheless, did you know that representatives of the BH army had categorically refused any discussion of an extension to that agreement? Were you certain at the time that they were about to launch an offensive? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: What I knew was that the agreement that existed was a compromise. A four-month agreement is a very modest result. My predecessors and I consistently tried to consult with all parties concerned regarding an agreement that would be valid for a far longer period. Unfortunately, we didn't succeed. I was not aware of any preparations for an offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about a specific piece of information or a fact, if you like. When you arrived, did you know about the tunnel beneath the Butmir airport? It was quite a long tunnel and was being used by the BH army. They brought medicine, food, and such like through the tunnel and into the city. That's what the tunnel was meant to be used for, but the tunnel was also used for bringing in enormous amounts of ammunition. Did you know about that while you were in Sarajevo, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Not immediately upon my arrival, but fairly soon after I had entered my position there I was notified of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in your capacity as an officer, know, and the rest of the UN people there, that the tunnel was being used all the time by the BH army in great numbers; that the tunnel was often used for them to leave Sarajevo and go to other theatres of war and then to go back to Sarajevo? Is this something that you were aware of at the time, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, in any case we presumed that that was also happening, but the tunnel was used very often to get supplies to the population because the other supply convoys were often blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I already said that naturally that was of vital importance for the residents of Sarajevo, and from this position I can say that I was happy for those people to receive medical supplies. However, what I was asking you about was that large numbers of troops used this tunnel to get out of the city and that UNPROFOR did nothing about it, to prevent it. I'm talking about the soldiers getting in and out. I have nothing against medical supplies and other merchandise to sustain people's lives. But why didn't UNPROFOR stop the troops getting in and out of what was supposed to be the demilitarised zone? I would like to hear your answer to this.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I cannot provide a specific answer as to what extent the BiH army used this tunnel. There were French battalions of the Sarajevo Sector located at the airports, and probably -- were probably able to see the tunnel, and I am not aware of the extent to which they observed the BH army used this tunnel. You'll have to ask this question to the people at Sector Sarajevo, because I never received any information about that in a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am interested to hear whether you knew that the entry and exit points were at places where there was a lot of civilian population.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The tunnel exit was on the side of the city. Yes, there were a lot of civilians there. But the other side near Mount Igman, no, there was no dense population there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Brigadier, your answer to the previous question suggests that you do have knowledge that the tunnel was used by the BiH army. The difficulty that you have is in identifying the extent to which the tunnel was used by the BH army. Is that a fair summary of your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not exactly. I'll try to be a bit more specific in my response. I did not receive any report that the BiH army was using the tunnel, but I'm not excluding that because we had had no permanent control over -- to supervise who entered or exited the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I put a question to Counsel Tapuskovic? I'm not sure I fully appreciate the question that you originally put to the witness, because -- are you suggesting that it would be a violation of the existing agreements if weapons were taken into Sarajevo through the tunnel? Would that be a violation; and, if so, a violation of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, weapons arrived in Sarajevo, that's one thing, but also fresh troops came into Sarajevo, and at times even the soldiers from Sarajevo would leave to other fronts at Igman and other areas and then they would go back to Sarajevo. At any rate, that constitutes a serious violation of the UN Resolution which, way back in 1993, declared this area a demilitarised zone. Had all this really been demilitarised, no one would have to do anything with weapons if that really had been demilitarised. And if there hadn't been such a huge amount of weapons and troops and constant incidents, nothing would have happened. Just like the case was in the situation in Kiseljak where the demarcation line was between the Croats and the Serbian army, there was no shooting there. That's the point. This is a serious violation of the UN Resolution because it had become increasingly a military issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have back on our monitors document DD00-0287.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to page 2 -- in fact, it's page 1, where you talk about the time when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, did you earlier ask the witness whether civilians were at the entrance and exit of the tunnel? I'm not quite sure whether you did; and, if you did, what the answer was to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My colleague reminded me of that, and I did ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As I understand, the entry point was an area which was densely populated. If I'm not mistaken, Mr. Witness, that's what you said. The entry point was where the civilian population was in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The tunnel has two ends. The tunnel end inside the city of Sarajevo was in a residential area, but the other end of the tunnel, at the side of Mount Igman, was not densely populated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Igman is pretty far away from this tunnel; is that correct? That's a mountain. That's a dominant mountain overlooking Sarajevo. It's not exactly at the exit point of the town. You need to travel for quite a long time from that point. I visited this area both when I was a child, and I also visited it as an adult and during the war. What you say is that there was just an entry and exit point. It depends on how you view it. If you're coming from the direction of Igman, that's an entry point. If you're going from Sarajevo, that's an entry point. It's difficult to discern between the two. However, both ends were civilian areas. The one in the city was completely a civilian area, but also the exit point from the tunnel, which was only 700 metres long, is in a populated area as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, but not as densely populated as the end that's on the Sarajevo side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand. But at both ends, whatever you take to be an entry point and an exit point, could have been a military target, when you have troops moving.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have in front of you page 1, or rather, page 2 of your statement given in 1996? Do you have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it now? I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is really going very slowly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have it, sir, in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, I still don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, that's document DD00-0287. And page 1 is actually page 2 of the document. Yes. This is exactly what we have on the monitors. Can you see it, sir, now?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In front of my -- in front of me I see the first page of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'd like to draw your attention to page 3 -- sorry, paragraph 3. You are talking about your arrival in Sarajevo, and you visited all the headquarters of all armies. You first visited the Croatian army, HVO; then the representatives of the BH army; and only after that, the representatives of the army of Republika Srpska in Pale. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, did you ever have contact with General Dragomir Milosevic, either by forwarding a protest directly to him or by talking to him on the phone or ever meeting him in person?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, that never happened. The counterpart of Mr. Milosevic was General Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph you say, somewhere in the middle: "My task was to make sure that the functions of BH command were carried out." I'm not going to ask you anything directly in this connection. I would just like to hear your comment. How do you understand and interpret this, that your task was to make sure that the functions of BH command were carried out? If I understand it correctly, you were on a peacekeeping mission there and you should have been interested in only what your mandate was, and that was to prevent conflicts, but you said what I just read out to you. Can you please comment on this?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, carrying out the duties of the Bosnia-Herzegovina command, but that covered a very broad range, from arranging for transport and evacuation of the wounded, exchanging prisoners of war, arranging humanitarian assistance, as well as ending hostilities by deploying military violence, and that was range of duties of the BH command, and as Chief of Staff, I contributed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a while ago I addressed one issue, but in the meantime I understood that there was a mistake take in the Serbian translation. It means a completely different thing in the English version. Therefore, it is not necessary for the General to give me any additional explanation, because I realise that it was a mistake in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I think we are still -- I think the General still has this statement in front of him. That's the English version of it. Page 2, last sentence, and then it moves on to the next page. I would like to ask you the following: You mentioned in the examination-in-chief that you had meetings with Mr. Silajdzic, the Prime Minister, sometime in May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the following, and I'm going to read it to you. You said as follows, that you had met with Silajdzic. And the last sentence you say: "During this meeting, Mr. Silajdzic was complaining about the shelling being carried out by the Bosnian Serbs in the area of the Jewish cemetery in Sarajevo." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That is one of the things that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- yes, but you told him, as it reads here: "We told him that on that particular day his troops had been provoking the shelling." Is this what you told him?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I will try to give a more extensive answer. The discussion was held to end the increased hostilities in the middle of May. We spoke to both parties on the phone to BSA in a meeting with the people from BiH. One of the subjects that were discussed was the shelling of the Jewish cemetery in Sarajevo. This incident had been provoked by BiH. That is what I told the persons present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But then you went on to say, and it can be seen from this statement, that Silajdzic was angry but, "I told him that due to the circumstances of the ABiH having started the firing incidents that morning, we could not use close-air support against the Bosnian Serbs on this occasion. But I also reminded him that we could use the air support against the Bosnians as well if they used their weapons in breach of the Security Council Resolution ..." and then you enumerate the relevant resolutions.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if I understand the question correctly. I tried to express that the use of violence by the UN was not only towards the Bosnian Serbs, but also in case of a breach by BiH, violence might be used against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the point was, on that morning that the use of close -- of artillery against the Serbs was out of the question because it was you who were provoking. Is that the gist of what you told him?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. It would be very unreasonable to punish the party that did not start and to leave the party that did start the hostilities unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I appreciate that. However, you had never attacked the BH army with the Rapid Reaction Force, not even on the 15th and 16th of June when the BH army offensive was launched and when they attacked all front lines. So the offensive started on the 15th and the 16th in which the BH army struck at all front lines. Not even then did you use or make any intervention in order to stop that.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The UN did not intervene at all hostilities. The policy was to try to intervene if the civilian population was in danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, in my view, this is an important area, and what you should be concentrating on is not whether UNPROFOR reacted to the BiH action but what was the nature of the BiH action and whether it called for defensive measures from the Bosnian Serbs. I'm not saying that UNPROFOR's conduct is entirely relevant, but you should be seeking to show that the Bosnian Serbs acted in a defensive way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, I can ask the General if this offensive started as it did, I wanted to ask him if that was an offensive with respect to which the Serbian side had to respond adequately to protect their front lines. I may ask him that. I think that, Judge Robinson, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I cannot tell for sure what answer is required from me. At any case, in the middle of May, a series of hostilities occurred; one time from BSA side and other occasions from BiH side. One specific occasion, in the case of the Jewish cemetery, it was started by BiH. When that was discussed, we said for that reason we will not attack BSA, but we will address BiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you didn't understand my question, General, nor the intervention by Judge Robinson. I'm not asking you about the action around the Jewish cemetery. I'm asking you about an all-out offensive launched on the 15th, 16th of June by the BH army on all fronts, and I'm sure that you were fully aware of that. And this offensive lasted for almost two months. What the Serbian army had to do in order to protect their troops and the civilians on their side, is that something that the army of the Republika Srpska had to do in response to that offensive, to launch certain actions of their own? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I still don't fully understand, but I want to stress that in not all cases when the warring sides were in conflict did the UN intervene. And sometimes it was impossible to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I do understand that on certain occasions it was impossible for UNPROFOR to intervene, but that wasn't what I asked you. I want you to explain to the Chamber whether everything that the Serbian army, after this two-month offensive, did was something that they had to do in order to protect their positions. That was my question. If I understand and if I'm not mistaken, that was the question posed to you by Judge Robinson as well.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I will not refuse to answer questions, but because of the translation, sometimes questions don't get clearly through to me. UNPROFOR had the impression that when someone was attacked he would defend himself. We would prefer the hostilities to be ceased, but not in all cases when fighting was going on did we intervene. And if defence is justified or not, that will be different from case to case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I just take you back to the statement which counsel referred you where you said, and I quote: "We told him that on this particular day his troops had been provoking the shelling." Are you able to tell us what form that provocation took? What did the Bosnian -- the BiH army do to provoke the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That morning they started shelling the BSA positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. They started shelling themselves. They started shelling the Bosnian Serbs. Yes. All right. Thanks. And the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- and the Bosnian Serbs responded with shelling. Shelling for shelling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Amongst others with mortars but also with small-calibre arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. However, I think the suggestion or the intervention made by General Dragomir Milosevic is warranted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind the General of an event which took place in June 1995 while this offensive was at its peak, the offensive launched by the BH army when the Rapid Force Reaction brigade of UNPROFOR was firing at Igman from Ilidza and hit the hospital Zica, in Blazuj, where people who came to visit their relatives in the hospital were killed. Does he remember this incident, and the protest lodged in this connection by the Serbian side? You intervened against a certain incident, I presume, by firing at the hospital. That's what UNPROFOR did. Do you remember that? Maybe it was a mistake of yours.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I remember an incident where a hospital was hit in Sarajevo during shellings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Bosniak Muslim hospital. I don't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was the hospital about a kilometre away from the ice stadium. And that hospital, as far as we could make certain, it had been hit by Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just one other matter, Mr. Tapuskovic. Where your case is that the action of the Bosnian Serbs was of a defensive character, then you should try to relate it to the incidents charged in the indictment, and don't leave it at a general level, as you have done here. For example, where, in the statement of the General, he says that: "We told him that on this particular day his troops had been provoking the shelling," it would be of importance to me to know whether that particular incident is captured in the indictment. I don't know whether it is. Or perhaps this is a matter that will be dealt with by you in greater detail in the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I can say is that the indictment does not include a single incident caused by the BH army. I would not like to deal with any comparison now. There's time enough for that. It was good that you reminded me of this. There is no mention of this incident or these incidents in the indictment whatsoever. I have now reached a point, having asked all those questions, where I will be moving on to perhaps the most important part of the general statement, the one that he made back in November 1996. That's why now I would like to please move on to what you have just been talking about, Mr. President, specific things that the witness can address in a specific manner. This is the English statement, page 3. Last paragraph of the English statement. Last paragraph. Have we got that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that before you, sir, the last paragraph? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I can't see whether this is the last paragraph because I have two paragraphs in front of me, and the bottom paragraph starts with: "I learned that the situation was not always what it seemed."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's the one I'm looking for. Yes. I will read that for you. "I learned that the situation was not always what it seemed." Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on to say -- is this correct, what you said? Indeed. And it goes on: "The shelling could be provoked by the Muslims or it could be an act of retaliation." That's what you said, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on: "Sometimes the BH army would fire mortars from their own barracks near the ice stadium." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The ice stadium is a civilian facility; right? I would like to draw your attention to paragraphs 14 and 15 of the other statement. I am compelled to tackle the matter like this simply because there is no other way to go around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about paragraph 16. I'm sorry. This is DD00-0319. Paragraph 15, and 14. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First things first. You need to have that before you. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I don't see any numbers on my text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 14. I have the English. Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: If you're referring to paragraph numbers, they don't appear on my monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The ice stadium.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Could you perhaps read aloud a sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is document -- well, first off, there you're filing a -- lodging a protest note with General Mladic. Is that it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Look, I'm talking about DD00-0319. This is the other statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us ensure that the statement to which you are referring is before the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I have paragraph 14 in front of me, from what I --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fourteen, paragraph 14. Yes. Yes. Down the middle of the paragraph. It's about you being in touch with General Mladic. "General Mladic does not deny the shelling. Rather, he says that his forces had been provoked into firing back." And then: "In mid-May there was generally a lot of shelling, and I recall that the area near the hospital and near the ice stadium were being shelled that day." Is that or is that not what you discussed with General Mladic, the way it's described in your statement, sir? Is that true, what we see here? Sorry? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please go to paragraph 15. "I remember --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Did you say General Mladic or General Milovanovic? Paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The translation says Mladic. I have Mladic in my B/C/S. It may have been Milovanovic, for all I know, but I don't think it makes any difference to my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The English has "Milovanovic." Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 -- let me go back to the shelling of the hospital. "I remember that there was an HQ of the Bosnian army near the ice stadium in that area, but I do not know what unit was the one in question. I recall that sometimes there was firing from mortars that were positioned at their HQ." And now the most important bit: "And I think it was inevitable that when firing back the nearby hospital might in fact be hit." Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. The text of my statement corresponds with what I alleged at the time, but I believe -- I do not believe that the text is entirely correct, because the hospital was about 1 kilometre away from the BiH barracks and therefore I believe that they could have avoided hitting the hospital. The aim would have been awfully -- would have needed to be awfully inaccurate to miss it by 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, sir, I must ask this: Which is true, then? When were you telling the truth, when this statement was recorded and you seemed quite definite about this, that it was inevitable that they should end up hitting the hospital. Or are you telling the truth now, that the hospital was about a kilometre away? Which is true? How do you account for this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsel, I may refer you to just further down in that same paragraph where the victim actually spells out --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So I think you shouldn't in any way allege that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- has not --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. However, I'm interested in this assessment, evaluation, that he provides. His take on it at the time seems to have been -- I don't have time to read the whole thing. I understand that things need to be seen in a given context, but he seemed quite definite when he stated that. "I think it was inevitable that when firing back the ... hospital might be hit." It is based on all the facts he provided later on. He seemed quite categorical about this. That's the only reason why I'm asking. Why did he make such a categorical statement at the time, Your Honours? I think we are owed an answer to that one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm willing to provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My statement is that, according to my memory, in 1996, the hospital was a bit closer to the BiH barracks than it later proved to be. I remembered it as being about 500 metres away, and in that case it would have been possible for a rather inaccurate aim to hit the hospital. During later interrogations, we consulted the map of Sarajevo and it turned out that it was located 1 kilometre away from the ice stadium; and then it becomes very unlikely to have such an inaccurate aim that you would hit the hospital when you fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm interested in the sequence of events. In paragraph 15, you say: "I think it is unavoidable that retaliatory fire might in fact hit the hospital which was nearby." And then the next sentence says: "I am shown on a map marked/numbered 0361-5780 by Investigator Hogan, and it appears that the hospital might be more than 500 metres, even up to 1 kilometre, away from the HQ." Were you shown the map immediately after you made the statement that "it was unavoidable that retaliatory fire might in fact hit the hospital which was nearby"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that exactly, because the investigator interrogated me on various occasions, and it's perfectly possible that I said the first time that it was inevitable and at one of the subsequent sessions he presented me with this map and then the text should have been adjusted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Be that as it may, today, in answer to my first question, you said that you accepted in its entirety your first statement. This was the other statement. I would now go back to where we left off, where you talked about the skating rink. Was this a civilian target? It's a skating rink. You normally get kids around a skating rink, or skaters. Or was this facility being used for a different purpose at the time in fact? We do know a thing or two about that, but I would like to hear your opinion, sir.

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The ice stadium was used at the time as a base for the company headquarters, namely, the UNPROFOR support staff. Adjacent to the ice stadium there was a BiH barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The ice stadium was used by the Danish company that supported the UNPROFOR headquarters, and adjacent to the ice stadium was a BiH barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: When you say "adjacent," what distance are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. We would need to consult the map. But it wouldn't have been more than 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do need to go back to DD00-0287. Can we please bring that up for the witness's benefit, the spot that we analysed a moment ago. That's page 3, the last paragraph at page 3. That's what we'll be talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I hope -- I hope so, because I see number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. That is DD00-0287. I'm talking about the November 1996 statement which I was showing you a while ago and then I had to go to that different one. This is page 3. It's the last paragraph in the English. We were looking at it a while ago. It reads: "I learnt that the situation was not always what it seemed." That's the reference that I'm talking about. Have you got that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, now I have the right text in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, we have concluded that the skating rink or the ice stadium was a facility used by UNPROFOR. And here you say: "The BH army would fire mortars from their own garrison near the ice stadium." You said that. You have just confirmed that for us. Does that mean that they were firing from there in order to hit you and in order to then blame the Serbs for the firing and the incident? Is that what they were doing? Can you answer that one?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: The assumption of UNPROFOR was that there was deliberate shooting near the UN installations installations in hopes that the Serbs would respond and would hit UN targets. This is based not only on this isolated incident. It happened regularly that there was firing in the immediate surroundings of UN positions by the BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then. You go on to clarify: "I saw the Bosnians firing mortars from near our headquarters using a small-calibre mobile mortar mounted on a vehicle with an open roof. This enabled it to move around the city and to fire from different positions." Is it true, what it says here, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you go on: "Very often these locations were very close to UN positions, that is, the PTT building (HQ Sector Sarajevo), the UNPROFOR Sarajevo headquarters, the Zetra ice stadium, and the Tito barracks." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And now we come to that problem, the one raised by the President, Mr. Robinson, at one point in time. It continues: "One mortar does not really give protection. Besides, if one wants to fire a mortar accurately, this takes time. One has to measure the position and such." And then it goes on to say: "The mobile mortar was more of a case of random shooting at Serb territory outside the town." Is it not true that the BH army soldiers were firing these shells randomly only in order to elicit a reaction from the army of Republika Srpska? Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That's the gist of the statement I made at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And then you repeat -- I won't be dwelling on that. "This be only be classed as provocation," but then you go on to say this -- you spoke about retaliation. Retaliation, that's what you say. "The Serbs fired back by firing many more shells at the city. For example, one mortar from the mobile mortar would result in several shells from Serb artillery positions." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That happened on various occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it was indispensable; you, as an artillery expert, of all people, should know that. It was indispensable not to fire a single shell, as done by the BH army men. You had to fire back several shells in order to stop an attack like that. If you just fired back one shell, that would have been a random act, too, an act of random firing. Please tell us, if you can: You said that representatives of the BH army would just fire a single shell and then leave. And that amounts to random firing, doesn't it? Is that right or not, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I alleged at the time it, and I still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were the Serbs -- yes. Yes, I do agree. But were the Serbs, for example, to respond by firing a single random shell at Sarajevo without targeting the specific target that had provoked them into firing to begin with? That would have achieved nothing at all. It takes several shells to target a certain facility. I think that is self-implicit. Or is your take on it quite different, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: No, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Same paragraph, further down, several lines down, you talk about the Serbs being able to see whatever they wished to see down there in the actual city from their firing positions. Isn't that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tour all the hills around the centre of Sarajevo where the BH army positions were? To name just some, Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo, Mojmilo to the north; particularly, Zuc, several other hills, Zuc, Hum and other such hills overlooking the city of Sarajevo? Were those positions not being used by the BH army position to control Sarajevo? They had it virtually in the palm of their hand. Can you confirm that for us, sir?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understood the question completely, but several of the BH army positions were perceptible to me. I could see them. Others could be seen from the positions of our observers, but there were other Serb positions that I never saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the Serb positions. I was asking you about the BH army positions at Zuc, Hum, and other hills. Did you see those? Debelo Brdo? Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, some the BH positions -- rather, most of them were visible at any rate to our observers, and if something happened there, then there would be a report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You are talking about the hills, are you, or not? I have no time to show you the map now. Are you talking about the BH army positions on those hills?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Well, around Sarajevo there were various positions of the BH army. Several, especially those near the centre of the city, were even visible from the UNPROFOR headquarters. Other positions were not visible from the headquarters but were visible to observers or by military people of the various UNPROFOR battalions stationed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were those BH army positions in the surrounding hills?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: In part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now come to that problem related to Markale. This is a significant issue, and I will take quite some time to deal with this. I think it's in everyone's best interest, and that applies to the Chamber, to be familiarised with this problem. I was trying to keep track of time, and I have tried to save most of my time for Markale. I would like to finish today's session by choosing a different subject matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Proceed. I'm not stopping you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, Your Honour. I may end today's sitting with a different topic, because for the other one I need quite a lot of time. If I don't have enough time, I could probably tackle another two brief issues. But I hope you will allow me to question the witness about this, and if you'll permit me to continue with that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I said I'm not stopping you. I've said that already. How you wish to use the time is a matter for you. It is clear to me that the two hours set were an underestimation of the time needed for this witness, who has evidence that is important to the case of both parties. Proceed. If you want to just deal with the two short topics, then do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I would move on to page 5 in the English version of this same statement. Page 5, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's paragraph 4. Can you see that, sir, in front of you? This is what you say here, if I can find it: "The cease-fire lasted until the end of April, after which the UN still tried to stop the shelling and sniping. I explained to the Bosnians we could only protect them against the shelling if it was not provoked." Is that what you said? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then two paragraphs down, you said: "In April the incidents of sniping started to increase." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you say here something quite interesting. I'm going to read the whole thing. "In my opinion, snipers were sometimes soldiers and sometimes renegades. If the military authorities cooperated, they could stop the sniping, because each boy and man had a weapon." You said each man, every man, not a soldier, had a weapon. Given that you were in Sarajevo, I would put it to you that you were not referring to the Serbian side but rather that every man and boy in Sarajevo had a weapon. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: That's correct. That's what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if we have time, but I would like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember an event in March when two young girls were killed at Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you ask him that, it seems to me that there is an issue arising out of that paragraph. You say: "Snipers were sometimes soldiers and sometimes renegades." What do you mean by "renegades"?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I mean they were non-military people. They were civilians who had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Non-military people, civilian with weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say: "If the military authorities cooperated, they could stop the sniping, although perhaps not for 100 per cent, as every man and boy had a weapon."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it fair to conclude from that statement that, as you said, in your opinion, it wasn't possible for the authorities to stop every incident of sniping?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I mean to say is -- I'm trying to -- what I mean to say is that the military authorities controlled their soldiers and are in a position to prevent their soldiers from acting as snipers. The military authorities do not control all civilians who have weapons. That was the intention of my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. I asked the question because the very next sentence appeared, in the absence of the explanation that you have just given, a little inconsistent, and that sentence is: "So the situation deteriorated because the authorities did not have the will to stop it. They did not take the necessary measures to stop it."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I mean that as well. Although it was virtually impossible to stop the sniping 100 per cent, it would have been possible to stop most of it if everybody had agreed to cooperate in that effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I understand now. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: General, your submission here about some of the snipers being civilians with weapons, did that apply to both the Bosnian Muslim population and the Bosnian Serb population? Or how is it to be understood? Were there civilian snipers on both sides that were not under the control of the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On both sides civilians had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Had weapons and used them in sniping incidents; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must assist once again. It says here, "Every man ..." He already explained that. We know about the soldier. But it says here even boys had weapons. Every boy had a weapon. And he was in Sarajevo at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That wasn't the question which he asked you to confirm, whether you were in Sarajevo. He asked you to confirm whether even boys had weapons, every boy had a weapon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a manner of speaking, yes. Many, many boys had weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Last question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I will keep it brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me take you to the paragraph after the next one. I'll just read it out to you and you can confirm whether yes or no. "One example of the Bosnian attitude was when Minister Muratovic complained about the sniping at a water distribution point and asked the UN for protection. When I asked where this water distribution point was, my interpreter explained that it was on Heroes Square, near the confrontation line, in full sight of the army of Republika Srpska. I told Muratovic that this was a way of provoking the sniping and suggested he move this water distribution point to a safer location." Is it all of this correct?

utterances.speaker: CORNELIS HENDRIK NICOLAI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 25th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
